stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers' conclusion?
stimulus: In a Norwegian fjord, common periwinkles from a sheltered inner site have shells about 30 percent thicker than periwinkles from an outer site near the fjord's mouth. The water at the inner site averages about 3°C warmer, and shore crabs, which crush periwinkles, are far more abundant there. In many mollusks, warmer water speeds shell deposition, so the difference could simply be a by-product of temperature. Marine biologist Sigrun Aasen and colleagues, however, concluded that the periwinkles thicken their shells in response to chemical cues released by crabs, not because of the warmer water.
choices: Surveys over several years found that inner-site periwinkles consistently had thicker shells and lived among more crabs than outer-site periwinkles did.
Outer-site periwinkles kept in crab-free tanks grew thicker shells when their water was warmed to the inner site's temperature than when it was not.
Outer-site periwinkles kept in tanks at the outer site's temperature grew thicker shells when given water that had held crabs than when given crab-free water.
Periwinkles taken from the outer site and caged at the inner site grew shells as thick as those of inner-site periwinkles within a single year.
explanation: The conclusion has two parts: crab cues cause the thickening, and warmth does not. To support both, a finding has to vary the crab cue while holding temperature fixed. Choice C does exactly that. Outer-site snails were kept at the colder outer-site temperature, and the only difference between the two groups was whether their water had held crabs. The cue group still grew thicker shells, so the cue alone produced the effect without any extra warmth.

A.why: This just restates the observation the passage starts with: thick shells and many crabs at the inner site. The researchers' explanation and the temperature explanation both predict this pattern, so it can't help you choose between them. You picked a finding that repeats the result instead of isolating its cause.

B.why: Here warmth alone, with no crabs, thickened the shells. That supports the alternative the researchers rejected, so it weakens their conclusion. You probably saw a controlled tank experiment with thicker shells and missed which variable was changed.

D.why: This is the trap for students who already know they need an experiment. Moving the snails to the inner site exposes them to more crabs and to warmer water at the same time. Their shells would thicken under either explanation, so the result can't show that crabs rather than temperature are responsible. You read support for one cause into a result that two causes explain equally well.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers' hypothesis?
stimulus: On dairy farms in western Ireland, barn swallow pairs nesting in barns that house cattle fledge more chicks per brood than pairs nesting in barns left empty. Cattle barns differ from empty ones in two relevant ways. Dung and animals attract large numbers of flies, a staple of nestling diets, and the cattle's body heat keeps the air several degrees warmer. Ornithologist Teodor Lindqvist and colleagues hypothesize that the swallows' advantage in cattle barns comes from the flies, which allow parents to bring food to nestlings more often, rather than from the added warmth.
choices: When fly traps cut fly numbers in cattle barns but left air temperature unchanged, both parents' feeding rates and fledging success fell toward empty-barn levels.
Within cattle barns, pairs that made more feeding trips per hour went on to fledge more chicks than did pairs in those barns that made fewer trips.
Throughout the nesting season, cattle barns held both far more flies and noticeably warmer air than did the empty barns on the same farms.
Parents in cattle barns and in empty barns made feeding trips at similar rates, but chicks in cattle barns lost less weight on cold nights.
explanation: Break the hypothesis into a chain and a rival. The chain runs from flies to more frequent feeding to more fledglings. The rival, warmth, is said not to be the cause. Choice A removes the first link (flies) while holding the rival (temperature) fixed. The middle link (feeding rate) and the outcome (fledging success) then both fall. That one finding supports every link in the chain and rules out warmth as the explanation.

B.why: This is the trap for students who see that feeding rate is the key link. It shows only that more feeding goes with more fledglings, and only inside cattle barns. It says nothing about whether flies cause the extra feeding. Warmer air could also free parents to make more trips. You confirmed one link of the chain and treated it as support for the whole hypothesis.

C.why: Both proposed causes are higher in cattle barns, which the passage already says. A finding that holds equally for both explanations can't separate them. You chose a statement that fits the hypothesis instead of one that singles out flies as the cause.

D.why: Similar feeding rates break the middle link the researchers depend on. Chicks staying heavier on cold nights points to warmth instead. This finding weakens the hypothesis. You may have noticed that cattle-barn chicks did better and missed which cause that benefit points to.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Haddad's hypothesis?
stimulus: Compression tights are widely thought to speed recovery between bouts of running by boosting circulation in the legs. In trials at her lab, runners wearing the tights did recover faster between repeated hill sprints than runners wearing loose shorts. Sports physiologist Noor Haddad suspects, however, that circulation is not the cause. She hypothesizes that the tights help by damping the vibration of the thigh muscles each time the foot strikes the ground, which limits the small-scale tissue damage that repeated impact produces.
choices: Runners wearing the tights recovered faster between hill sprints than runners wearing loose shorts of the same weight did.
Blood flow in the thigh muscles was about 15 percent higher in runners wearing the tights than in runners wearing loose shorts.
In cyclists, whose legs take almost no impact, the tights raised thigh blood flow as much as in runners but did not speed recovery.
Runners wearing the tights recovered faster and, according to motion sensors, had less thigh vibration at each foot strike.
explanation: Haddad's hypothesis has two parts: damping vibration from impact is what helps, and better circulation is not. To support it, a finding has to pull the two apart. Cyclists' legs take almost no impact, so the tights have no vibration to damp. They still raise blood flow just as much, yet recovery doesn't improve. Circulation alone isn't enough to produce the benefit, which points to impact damping.

A.why: You chose the observed result, which the passage already reports. It shows that the tights help but says nothing about why, so it can't favour vibration over circulation.

B.why: You picked a finding about circulation, the explanation Haddad rejects. Higher blood flow fits the common view at least as well as hers, and nothing here links the benefit to vibration.

D.why: You saw the right mechanism and stopped. In these runners the tights also boost circulation, so less vibration and faster recovery happen together with higher blood flow. The finding can't tell which one caused the faster recovery.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the team's conclusion?
stimulus: Streams with beaver dams often keep flowing through late summer, when nearby undammed streams run dry. One explanation is that the ponds behind the dams store surface water and release it slowly. Hydrologist Elena Sokolova proposes a different route: by spreading water across the floodplain, the dams raise the local water table, and groundwater then seeps back into the channel below the dam for weeks after inflow stops. Her team concluded that this groundwater pathway, not pond storage, is what sustains the late-summer flow.
choices: In August, dammed streams were still flowing at most survey points, whereas nearby undammed streams had stopped flowing entirely.
Below dams whose ponds had already drained by August, flow continued wherever floodplain wells showed the water table was still raised.
Ponds behind the dams held more water in early July than the streams below them carried over the whole month of August.
Floodplain water tables stood higher along dammed streams than undammed ones, and the dams' ponds stayed full well into August.
explanation: The conclusion makes two claims: groundwater sustains the flow, and pond storage does not. Once a pond has drained, it has no stored water left to release, so pond storage can't explain flow below it. If flow continues there, and only where the water table is still raised, the flow is tied to groundwater and the rival explanation is removed.

A.why: You chose a restatement of the observed difference between dammed and undammed streams. Both explanations predict this result, so it can't favour one.

C.why: You chose evidence that the ponds hold enough water to supply August flow. That supports pond storage, the explanation the team rejects.

D.why: You noticed the raised water table but missed that full ponds were present too. With both possible sources in place, this finding can't show which one keeps the stream flowing.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Vermeer's conclusion?
stimulus: Engineers sometimes embed capsules of dormant bacterial spores in concrete. When a crack lets in water, the spores revive and precipitate calcium carbonate, which seals the crack. But concrete can partly heal without bacteria: unreacted cement grains exposed in a crack also form calcium carbonate, and the capsules' cement-based shells could supply such grains. Materials scientist Ilse Vermeer tested samples that differed only in whether their capsules held live or heat-killed spores. She concluded that the bacteria, not the capsule shells, account for most of the sealing.
choices: Cracks in samples with live spores were filled with calcium carbonate along their full depth after four weeks in water.
Cracks in samples with live or heat-killed spores closed far more fully than cracks in samples containing no capsules.
Cracks closed more fully in samples kept submerged in water than in otherwise identical samples kept in dry air.
Cracks in samples with heat-killed spores closed little more than those in capsule-free concrete, while live-spore cracks closed fully.
explanation: The heat-killed samples have the same capsule shells but no working bacteria. If those samples barely outperform concrete with no capsules at all, the shells add little. If the live-spore samples seal fully, the bacteria account for the difference. This choice compares the two conditions the way the conclusion needs.

A.why: You matched calcium carbonate to the bacteria. The passage says unreacted cement grains form the same mineral, so finding it in the cracks doesn't show which process put it there.

B.why: You chose a result that holds for both capsule groups. If dead-spore capsules seal almost as well as live ones, the shells may be doing the work. That points away from Vermeer's conclusion.

C.why: Both healing processes need water, so better sealing under water fits either explanation. It doesn't separate bacteria from shells.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ferreira's hypothesis?
stimulus: Volunteers were given one of two breakfast drinks matched in volume and calories. One was thickened with viscous guar gum, and the other contained an equal mass of non-viscous cellulose fiber. At lunch three hours later, volunteers ate less after the guar drink. Nutrition scientist Tomás Ferreira hypothesizes that guar reduced intake because its thick gel slowed the rate at which the stomach emptied, prolonging the stretch signals that suppress appetite.
choices: When given with a compound that speeds stomach emptying, the guar drink no longer reduced lunch intake relative to the cellulose drink.
Both the guar drink and the cellulose drink left the stomach more slowly than an equal volume of plain water did.
Volunteers ate less at lunch after the guar drink whether they had eaten a large or a small dinner the night before.
Volunteers who ate the least at lunch after the guar drink also rated it as the thickest and most filling drink.
explanation: Ferreira proposes a chain: guar leads to slower stomach emptying, which leads to eating less. If the middle link is that cause, removing it should remove the effect. Speeding emptying back up erases guar's advantage, so this finding isolates slow emptying as the cause.

B.why: You found the right mechanism but in both groups. If both drinks slow emptying, slow emptying can't explain why only guar reduced lunch intake.

C.why: You chose evidence that the result holds up across conditions. It confirms that guar reduces intake again but says nothing about why.

D.why: You linked perceived thickness to eating less. How thick or filling a drink feels is not how fast the stomach empties, so the proposed mechanism is never tested.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the meteorologists' conclusion?
stimulus: Summer afternoon storms drop more rain on the area east of Halvorsen, downwind of the city, than on similar countryside to its west. Two features of the city could explain this. Its pavement and buildings heat the air above them, driving stronger updrafts. Its traffic and industry also emit aerosol particles on which cloud droplets can form. After analyzing two decades of radar data, meteorologists concluded that the rainfall increase is driven mainly by the city's heat, not by its aerosols.
choices: Over the two decades, summer afternoon rainfall east of Halvorsen exceeded rainfall west of the city by about a fifth.
Rainfall rose on hot afternoons both east and west of Halvorsen, and by similar amounts in the two areas.
On weekends, when the city's aerosol emissions fell sharply but its surface heating did not, rain east of the city stayed just as elevated.
The rainfall increase east of the city was largest on its hottest days, which were also the days when its air was most polluted.
explanation: To show that heat, not aerosols, drives the increase, you need conditions where one changes and the other doesn't. On weekends aerosols drop but heating stays the same. If downwind rain doesn't fall, aerosols aren't needed for the increase, which leaves heat.

A.why: You chose a figure for the observed increase. It confirms that the effect exists but doesn't say what causes it.

B.why: You chose a pattern that appears both east and west of the city. Something true of both areas equally can't explain why only the downwind area gets extra rain.

D.why: You noticed that the increase follows heat, which fits the conclusion. But the hottest days were also the most polluted, so aerosols rise with heat and the finding can't separate the two.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Mensah's conclusion?
stimulus: Ocean acidification slows shell growth in many bivalves, but a parent's experience may shape how its offspring cope. Marine biologist Akosua Mensah raised rock oysters in either acidified or normal seawater. She then reared the larvae of each group in both conditions. She concluded that parental exposure specifically prepared offspring for acidified water, rather than simply producing larvae that were more vigorous overall.
choices: Larvae of exposed parents grew faster than larvae of unexposed parents in acidified water and in normal seawater alike.
Larvae of exposed parents outgrew those of unexposed parents in acidified water, but the two grew equally in normal seawater.
Larvae of both exposed and unexposed parents grew more slowly in acidified water than they did in normal seawater.
Adults kept in acidified water built thinner shells than adults kept in normal seawater over the same period.
explanation: The conclusion has two parts. Offspring of exposed parents should do better in acidified water, and that advantage should not appear in normal water, because an advantage everywhere would just be general vigour. Only this choice shows both: an advantage in acidified water and none in normal seawater.

A.why: You checked the acidified-water half and stopped. An advantage in both kinds of water is exactly the overall vigour that Mensah's conclusion rules out.

C.why: You chose a result that holds for both groups of larvae. It shows that acidification slows growth but doesn't compare offspring of exposed and unexposed parents.

D.why: This describes the parents, not the offspring. The conclusion concerns how parental exposure affects the next generation.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Raman's conclusion?
stimulus: Wheat planted along hedgerows often outyields wheat in the open centers of the same fields. Hedgerows slow the wind, which reduces water loss from the crop's leaves. They also house parasitoid wasps that lay eggs in aphids, killing these sap-feeding pests before their numbers build. Agronomist Priya Raman concluded that the yield gain in her study fields came chiefly from the wasps' suppression of aphids rather than from shelter from the wind.
choices: Wheat growing beside the hedgerows yielded more grain per hectare than wheat growing in the open centers of the fields.
Wind speeds over wheat beside the hedgerows were lower than wind speeds over wheat growing in the field centers.
Hedgerows netted so that wasps could not reach the wheat still cut wind speed over the adjacent wheat by about half.
Beside hedgerows netted so that wasps could not reach the wheat, the wheat yielded no more than wheat in the field centers.
explanation: Raman credits the wasps rather than the windbreak, so the evidence has to remove one and keep the other. Netting keeps the wasps out while the hedgerow still blocks wind. If the yield gain disappears under those conditions, wind shelter alone doesn't produce it, and the wasps do.

A.why: You chose the observed yield gain, which the passage already reports. Both explanations predict it, so it doesn't favour Raman's.

B.why: You chose evidence for the wind-shelter mechanism, the one Raman downplays. Calmer air near hedgerows fits the rival explanation, not hers.

C.why: You recognised the right experiment but chose its setup instead of its result. Knowing that netted hedgerows still block wind tells you nothing until you know what happened to the yield.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Svensson's claim?
stimulus: Probate inventories from the Lowland towns show that the share of households owning printed cotton rose sharply in the 1780s, displacing woolen worsted. Many historians attribute the change to fashion, spread by illustrated magazines that praised light printed fabrics. Historian Margit Svensson argues instead that the decisive factor was price: a canal opened in 1779 cut the cost of shipping cotton cloth to towns along its route.
choices: Printed cotton ownership rose in the 1780s in canal towns but stayed flat in nearby towns off the canal where the magazines circulated equally.
In canal towns, printed cotton cost less in the 1780s than in the 1770s, and magazines praising it were widely read there as well.
Magazines praising printed fabrics reached canal towns and towns off the canal in roughly equal numbers during the 1780s.
By 1790, inventories in the Lowland towns listed printed cotton in more households than they listed woolen worsted.
explanation: Svensson's claim holds only if the canal's price cut, not fashion, explains the rise. The towns off the canal had the same magazines but not the cheaper shipping. If ownership rose only in canal towns, fashion alone wasn't enough, and the cost difference accounts for the change.

B.why: You saw the price drop, which is Svensson's factor. But the magazines were also widely read in those same towns, so the finding can't show which one drove the change.

C.why: You chose a fact that is equally true of both kinds of town and gives no ownership figures. Without knowing what people bought, it can't link the rise to price.

D.why: You chose a restatement of the observed shift from worsted to cotton. Both explanations predict it, so it adds no support for Svensson.
